definition: Because every dispatched generator earns the same market clearing price, a plant can safely bid very low (passive) without losing revenue as long as some other participant sets a higher price; deliberately bidding to push the price up (active) is riskier because it raises the chance of not clearing at all.
core_idea: The choice between active and passive bidding comes down to how much profit a plant would forgo if it failed to clear, which depends on the spread between the market price and the plant's own production cost.
key_points: In a uniform-price auction there is no need to be the top bidder — a plant earns the clearing price regardless of how low it bid, provided someone else sets a higher price.
Actively bidding to try to raise the market price carries real risk: an aggressive bid can fail to clear, meaning the plant earns nothing for that period.
The decision to bid actively hinges on how much profit is at stake if the plant ends up inactive.
A plant's profit is the spread between the market price and its own cost of production, so low-cost plants risk giving up much more profit than high-cost plants by going inactive.
trading_implications: Low-cost producers should generally favor passive, low bids to guarantee dispatch and protect their large profit margin.
Higher-cost, thinner-margin producers have comparatively less to lose from occasional non-dispatch, so they have more incentive to bid aggressively to try to move the price up.
